qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lectures thirteen and fourteen. Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms. This is how to search for good trade-offs.
Two wind turbines stand in a row. The back one sits in the slow air behind the front one, its wake.
The back turbine sits in the front one's wake.
Now the back turbine moves further away. Its power climbs from seventy-seven to ninety-five per cent.
Moving it further back gives it more power.
But the longer cable costs more, from three million pounds to twelve.
But the longer cable costs more money.
We want low cost and high power, and one gets worse as the other improves. That is a trade-off.
Cost and power pull against each other: a trade-off.
Now take a whole wind farm. Each layout gets two scores, cost and power.
Each layout gets two scores: its cost and its power.
Layout A costs twenty million and makes thirty megawatts. That pair is its objective vector, one point on the plot.
Layout A becomes one point, its objective vector: (20, 30).
Layout E costs fifty-two million but makes seventy megawatts.
Layout E costs more but makes more power: (52, 70).
Eleven layouts give eleven points. Up and to the left is better.
Eleven layouts, eleven points. Better is up and to the left.
Let us compare two layouts, D and G.
Compare two layouts, D and G.
D costs less than G, and it makes more power too.
D is cheaper and makes more power.
G sits in D's box, where everything is worse on both goals. So D dominates G.
So D dominates G: no worse on any goal, better on at least one.
Now D and K. D is cheaper, but K makes more power.
Now D and K: D is cheaper, but K makes more power.
Each wins on one goal, so neither dominates. They are mutually non-dominating.
Neither wins on both: they are mutually non-dominating.
Which layouts does no other layout dominate?
Which layouts does no other layout dominate?
Five layouts turn red. Each one is beaten by a cheaper, stronger layout.
Five layouts are each beaten by another one: they turn red.
The six left over form the Pareto front.
The six left over form the Pareto front.
So there is no single best layout. The answer is a set of trade-offs.
So the answer is a whole set of layouts, not one best.
Here are twelve solutions. This time both goals are minimised, so better is down and to the left.
Twelve solutions, both goals minimised.
The five points that nobody dominates get rank zero.
Rank 0: the ones that nobody dominates.
Set them aside. The non-dominated points that are left form rank one.
Set them aside: the next front of what is left is rank 1.
Keep peeling, like an onion. Then come rank two and rank three.
Keep peeling, like an onion: rank 2, then rank 3.
Now every solution has a rank, and a lower rank is better.
Every solution now has a rank: lower is better.
A front can hold many points. Which ones should we keep?
Inside one front, which points should we keep?
The two ends get a crowding distance of infinity, so they are always kept.
The two ends get infinity: they are always kept.
For Q, draw a box out to its neighbours, P and R. Its size works out at nought point seven five.
For Q, draw a box out to its neighbours P and R: 0.75.
R scores one, and S scores one point two five.
R and S get bigger boxes: 1.00 and 1.25.
Bigger boxes win. That keeps the front spread out.
Prefer the biggest box: it keeps the front spread out.
NSGA-II starts with N parents. Here N is six.
NSGA-II starts with N = 6 parents.
The parents breed six children, shown in purple.
They breed six children.
Parents and children go into one pool of twelve.
Parents and children are merged: 12 in all.
Non-dominated sorting splits the twelve into ranks.
Non-dominated sorting splits the 12 into ranks.
Rank zero, A, B and C, fits into the six places whole.
Rank 0 fits whole: A, B and C are kept.
Rank one has four members for three places. Crowding decides, and E has the smallest box, so E is dropped.
Rank 1 has four for three places: crowding drops E.
The rest are discarded. Because parents compete with their children, the best are never lost. That is elitism.
The best always survive to the next generation: elitism.
One solution dominates another when it is no worse on any goal and better on one.
Non-dominated sorting peels the population into fronts, like an onion.
NSGA-II merges parents and children, sorts them, and keeps the best N.
